R0035.title: Login Credential Reuse
R0035.definition: Copying a user's session credentials (session cookies) to another device to bypass the login process and directly reuse the user's identity.
R0035.description: A common method is to obtain user cookies to enable automated password-free login. Many account vendors sell accounts by providing only login cookies rather than credentials — known as CK trading. CK trading can bypass SMS verification code login and prevents buyers from changing passwords, enabling multiple resales of the same account.
R0035.influence: Bypasses MFA multi-factor authentication mechanisms in the login process, or enables a single account to log in on multiple devices.

references.title: Steal Web Session Cookie - MITRE ATT&CK T1539

observables: The same account's session cookie is used concurrently across multiple different devices/IPs/locations
After login, the MFA multi-factor verification flow is skipped and the session state directly enters business operations
Account vendors bulk-sell accounts providing only CK (cookies), with login behavior showing no password entry or verification code step

R0035-002.title: Session Fixation Attack
R0035-002.definition: An attacker makes a user use a session identifier known to or controlled by the attacker before login, then reuses that session after the user authenticates to take over the account.
R0035-002.description:
Session fixation occurs when an application keeps the same Session ID before and after login, accepts session identifiers injected through URLs, forms, or cross-subdomain cookies, or fails to regenerate sessions after authentication and privilege changes. The attacker first causes the victim to visit a link or page carrying a fixed session identifier, waits for the victim to log in, and then uses the same session identifier in the authenticated state.

Unlike session token theft, the attacker does not necessarily need to steal the user's cookie afterward; the controlled session is fixed into the user's browser in advance. If the platform lacks post-login session rotation, cookie domain isolation, SameSite/HttpOnly/Secure settings, and anomalous-session detection, attackers can bypass protections after password and MFA login and perform sensitive actions such as transactions, password changes, card binding, or data export.
R0035-002.influence: Attackers can reuse the fixed session after the user authenticates to take over the account, bypassing login and MFA flows and causing account control, transaction tampering, sensitive data access, and financial loss.

observables: The Session ID does not change between the pre-login and post-login states
A user enters from an external link containing SID, session, token, or similar session parameters and then completes login
The same session identifier is immediately reused by another device or IP after the victim logs in
A cross-subdomain cookie or controllable response header sets a session cookie accepted by the business domain

R0035-001.title: Login Credential Theft
R0035-001.definition: Stealing user identity credentials to impersonate the user's identity for unauthorized access.
R0035-001.description: Credential theft is a form of credential reuse (R0035). Credential reuse more often refers to a voluntary process of copying and reusing credentials; credential theft refers to a user's identity credentials being stolen by a hacker for use elsewhere to impersonate the user's login.
R0035-001.influence: Many account systems do not invalidate existing login sessions after a password change, meaning that with stolen or reused cookies, a hacker can maintain persistent login access to the target user's account.

references.title: Nearly 1,000 Data Breaches in Q1 2023, Affecting 1,204 Companies Across 38 Industries
Credential Stuffing Prevention Cheat Sheet - OWASP

observables: Old sessions remain valid after the account password is changed, with login state not revoked
User session cookies appear in infostealer-leaked data or dark-web trading
The same account logs in from a foreign location or anomalous device, with behavior deviating from the user's historical profile
